common_name: Honka Pink Dahlia (Star-Shaped Pink Orchid-Flowered Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the danger of frost has passed; Honka Pink is a Dutch-bred orchid-flowered dahlia with narrow, rolled petals that give its star-shaped blooms an open, airy look quite different from a double decorative flower.

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in well-drained soil with the growth eye facing up, and stake the slender stems in windy sites. Honka Pink produces 3-4 inch, medium-to-dark pink star-shaped flowers with rolled petal edges and a bright yellow central disc that stays open to pollinators, unlike most fully double dahlia forms. Plants branch freely and bloom prolifically from midsummer through the first hard frost, making excellent cut flowers with minimal disbudding needed. Lift and store tubers after foliage is blackened by frost in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Tohsuikyoh Dahlia (Blush-Pink Fading to Cream Double Orchid Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Tohsuikyoh is a Japanese double orchid-flowered dahlia introduced by Ohta in the early 1960s, prized for its soft color transition as blooms age.

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in rich, free-draining soil, spacing plants to allow good air circulation around the tall stems. Tohsuikyoh opens with a delicate pink blush that gradually fades to creamy white, its double orchid-form blooms made of narrow, slightly rolled petals arranged in a looser, airier double than a standard decorative dahlia. Stake stems early, as the 4-foot plants can be top-heavy once in full bloom from midsummer to frost. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Ryecroft Jim is a pink-flowered sibling to the better-known Ryecroft Marge, carrying the same anemone-flowered structure of pincushion-like tubular florets ringed by flat outer petals.

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in well-drained soil with the growth eye facing up, spacing plants to let the bushy habit fill in. Ryecroft Jim bears pink outer ray florets surrounding a dense, raised yellow pincushion center, giving each bloom the double-tiered look characteristic of anemone-flowered dahlias. The open centers attract pollinators more readily than fully double dahlia forms, and the plant flowers continuously from midsummer to frost. Deadhead regularly and lift tubers for storage once frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Asahi Chohje Dahlia (Red-and-White Striped Anemone-Flowered Dahlia, AGM)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Asahi Chohje is a Japanese anemone-flowered dahlia introduced in the early 1960s and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable garden performance.

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in moderately fertile, well-drained soil, staking the 4-foot stems as flower buds form. Asahi Chohje produces bright red-and-white striped outer ray florets surrounding a dense boss of shorter tubular florets, giving each anemone-form bloom a distinctive bicolor, pincushion-centered look. It flowers abundantly from midsummer through the first autumn frosts and holds up well as a cut flower. Lift and store tubers after foliage blackens with frost in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Anna Lindh Dahlia (Pearly White Waterlily Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Anna Lindh is a tall, clump-forming waterlily dahlia with broad, shallow petals that stay flatter and less layered than a decorative or ball type.

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in well-drained soil, staking stems in exposed sites since the large flat blooms can catch wind. Anna Lindh bears large, fully double pearly-white waterlily-form flowers with broad, saucer-shaped ray florets that are only lightly involute along their edges, giving each bloom a shallow, water-lily-like profile over dark, serrated foliage. It blooms profusely from midsummer until the first frosts and makes a long-lasting cut flower. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Le Castel Dahlia (White Waterlily Dahlia Blushed Pink with Age, AGM)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Le Castel was raised by French hybridizer Louis Laurent and holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable, long-stemmed waterlily blooms.

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in rich, free-draining soil; the long, strong stems of Le Castel make it a favorite for cutting gardens. Flowers open neat white and 4-6 inches across, with broad, shallow waterlily-form petals that take on a light pink flush as the bloom ages and matures over several days. Plants bloom continuously from midsummer to autumn frost over dark green foliage. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Minnpink Chrysanthemum (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Cushion Mum, Rose Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; Minnpink was named in the University of Minnesota's cold-hardy mum program and was recognized as a top garden performer shortly after its release.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Minnpink forms a tidy, dome-shaped cushion mound without pinching. Fully double, bright rose-pink decorative flowers open in early-to-mid September, timed to color up reliably even in short-season northern gardens, and the blooms hold more than two weeks in a vase with floral preservative. Its University of Minnesota breeding gives it outstanding winter hardiness compared to typical florist mums. Lift and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

common_name: Minnautumn Chrysanthemum (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Cushion Mum, Bronze)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; Minnautumn is part of the University of Minnesota's cold-hardy cushion mum series and is one of the later-blooming members of that program.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Minnautumn grows into a dense, rounded mound and does not need pinching to stay compact. Warm bronze, fully double decorative flowers with golden-copper overtones cover the plant in mid-October, later than most Minn-series siblings, over fragrant, ferny dark green foliage. Its University of Minnesota breeding gives it outstanding winter survival without mulch in cold-winter regions. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Morden Candy Chrysanthemum (Cold-Hardy Canadian Prairie Mum, Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; Morden Candy was bred at the Morden Research Station in Manitoba, part of the same Agriculture Canada program as Morden Cameo and Morden Garnet, for exceptional prairie winter hardiness.

directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Morden Candy grows into an upright, spreading clump of fragrant ferny foliage. Fully double, bright pink daisy flowers with rose overtones smother the stem tips from early to late fall, blooming reliably even in short prairie growing seasons. Its Agriculture Canada breeding gives it outstanding winter hardiness to Zone 3 without winter mulch. Cut plants back in early spring before new growth resumes, and divide overgrown clumps every two to three years.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; Starlet belongs to the Korean-type garden chrysanthemum group and the NCS Class 9 Spoon bloom form, in which each ray floret opens into a small spoon-shaped tip.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Starlet forms a tidy, dense cushion mound that needs little or no pinching. Honey-bronze flowers cover the plant profusely in fall, each daisy-like bloom made of narrow, tubular ray florets that flare into a small rounded spoon at the tip, distinguishing it from standard single or decorative mums. It is a favorite for autumn container plantings and informal arrangements where its unusual petal shape stands out. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the danger of hard frost has passed; Chatsworth is grown in the National Chrysanthemum Society's spray classification (Class 21b), where each stem is left to branch naturally and produce multiple blooms rather than being disbudded to one flower.

directions: Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants about 18 inches apart; unlike exhibition types, spray mums like Chatsworth are left undisbudded so each stem branches into a spray of blooms. Flowers are a rich orange-bronze double form, produced in generous sprays that make it a popular choice for both garden display and cutting. Pinch young plants once in late spring to encourage branching, and stake tall stems before the flower sprays become heavy. In colder zones, treat as a cut-flower annual or overwinter divisions under cover.
